raw_text:
- Investigating why repeated responses to the same question differ
- Observable factors contributing to variation in responses: context, time, emotional state, cognitive load
- Observed differences: logical consistency, frequency of errors, cognitive load assessment techniques

Assumptions
- Responses to questions are influenced by context and mental state
  
Research design
- Cross-sectional study design: gather data on responses under varied contexts and mental states
- Test-retest design: collect data on responses to the same question under differing conditions over time

Data or evidence needed
- Data on context during response
- Data on time of response
- Data on emotional state during response
- Data on cognitive load during response
- Data on logical consistency of responses
- Data on error frequency of responses
- Data on cognitive load assessment techniques

Measurement
- Checklists for context assessment
- Time logs for response time
- Self-report scales for emotional state
- Cognitive load measurements (e.g., working memory tasks)
- Logic tests for logical consistency
- Error count recordings

Analysis
- Statistical tests to examine relationships among context, time, and error rate
- Linear regression to analyze the effect of context, time, and emotions on error frequency and logical consistency
- Analysis of variance to examine differences in cognitive load among conditions

Decision / stopping rule
- Stopping rule: data saturation (minimal change in insights after collecting a certain number of responses)
- Decision rule: based on analysis, variation in responses explained by one or more factors, significant differences in context or cognitive load

Limitations
- Limited generalizability due to sample size
- Potential for recall bias in self-reported emotional states
- No control over spontaneous cognitive load changes
- Limited ethical standards in testing cognitive load through working memory tasks
